sections.title: Sniff, by QuantBase
sections.text:
**Sniff any coin before you buy.** Paste a pump.fun meme coin and Sniff tells you who made it, who paid the
wallet that made it, what else those people launched, and how those coins ended. It walks a FalkorDB graph of
632,339 pump.fun launches and 424,007 wallets. Claude writes the answer, and every sentence in it links to the
part of the graph that proves it. Sniff shows history, not predictions.

Entry for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB **Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents**, Tracks 01, 02 and 03.
Team **QuantBase**. Built during the event window, Oct 15–18, 2026 (IST).

sections.title: The graph (`lineage`)
sections.text:
```mermaid graph LR W[Wallet] -- CREATED --> C[Coin] W2[Wallet] -- FUNDED --> W H[Hub
exchange-like, dead end] -- FUNDED --> W S[Wallet
early buyer] -- SNIPED --> C C -- LINKS --> X[Handle
X, Telegram, website] W -- IN_RING --> R[Ring] ``` | Node | Count | What it is | |---|---|---| | Coin | 632,339 | a pump.fun launch (other launchpads dropped) | | Wallet | 424,007 | creators, their funders, early buyers | | Hub | 89 | wallets that funded more than 200 others (exchanges, big farms) | | Handle | 33,009 | a social account or website domain used on a coin | | Ring | 6,556 | wallets and coins joined by funding and creation (≥ 2 creators) | 1,089,444 nodes and 1,513,175 relationships load in 30 s with the FalkorDB bulk loader (521 MB in memory).

sections.title: The agent
sections.text:
```mermaid graph TD Q[Question or coin] --> L[Claude Sonnet 5.5
up to 8 tool calls] L -- tool call --> T[9 read-only tools
fixed Cypher on FalkorDB] T -- rows + evidence ids E1, E2… --> L L --> V[Answer, 2–5 sentences,
each citing an E id] V --> K[Citation check
unknown or off-topic ids removed] K --> U[App: answer + map that lights up each E id] T -. no key or AI error .-> D[Fixed dossier from the same tools] D --> U ``` - **Tools** (`app/tools.py`): `search_coins`, `coin_dossier`, `funding_trail`, `siblings`, `shared_snipers`, `shared_handles`, `ring`, `connect`, `top_operators`. Each one is a fixed, parameterised, read-only Cypher query (`app/queries.py`); the model never writes Cypher. - **Evidence ids:** every tool result carries ids (`E1`, `E2`, …) naming the nodes and edges behind it. - **Checked citations:** a sentence may only cite an id that a tool really returned, and only from a tool that can show that kind of claim (a sentence about socials must cite `shared_handles`). Anything else is removed, and a sentence left with no valid citation is dropped. A tool that finds nothing returns a "none found" id, so "no other coin reuses its socials" is cited too. - **No key, or the AI is down:** a fixed dossier built from the same tools answers instead. The facts never depend on the model. - **Wording:** answers describe history only and end with the base rate: 3.7% of the launches in this graph graduated.

sections.title: Why a graph
sections.text:
- **Money moves in hops.** "Who paid the wallet that made this coin, and who else did they pay?" is a 2–3 hop
  walk. In SQL it's a pile of self-joins; in Cypher it's one pattern.
- **Hubs are dead ends.** An exchange funds thousands of wallets, so walking through it links everyone to
  everyone. Hubs are their own label with no incoming funding edges, and no query walks through them.
- **Rings** come from `algo.WCC` over funding and creation edges. 3,824 of the 3,900 multi-creator clusters
  that our collector found by other means fall entirely inside one ring.
- **"How are these two connected?"** is `algo.SPpaths`, with hubs and platform-sized handles filtered out.

sections.text:

sections.title: Use Sniff from your own agent (MCP)
sections.text:
The nine lineage tools plus `memory_recall`, `memory_note` and `brain_ask` are served over MCP (streamable
HTTP). No AI key is needed to call them. Lineage reads also save scanned public evidence in `memory`;
`memory_note` writes a public agent observation. Calls are rate-limited per IP.

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http sniff https://sniff.quantbase.live/mcp
```

Any client that takes a JSON config:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "sniff": { "type": "http", "url": "https://sniff.quantbase.live/mcp" } } }
```

Then ask: "Use sniff to check who is behind `<mint>`." Every result carries evidence ids to cite.

MCP results include a random `session_id`. Pass it on subsequent lineage calls to reuse recorded evidence.
`memory_recall(entity="coin:<mint>")` shows anonymised cross-session findings;
`memory_recall(session="<session_id>")` opens one session. Another agent can add
`memory_note(entity="coin:<mint>", by="quantbase-trading-agent", text="A public observation")`.
The agent label is self-declared, and a note never becomes verified lineage evidence.

sections.title: API
sections.text:
- `POST /api/ask {"question": "...", "mint": "<optional>", "session_id": "<optional>"}`: JSON, or server-sent
  events (`step`, `evidence`, `verdict`, `done`) with `Accept: text/event-stream`. A random HttpOnly cookie
  carries the session in the browser. Neither visitor questions nor network addresses are saved in memory.
- `GET /api/memory?entity=coin:<mint>` or `?session=<session_id>`: findings and the memory graph; with no
  parameter uses the browser's session.
- `POST /api/brain/ask {"question": "How does QuantBase handle paper vs live?"}`: cited public source
  excerpts, full source sections and a knowledge graph. No runtime AI call is needed.
- `GET /api/brain`: corpus sources, fetch dates and extraction modes.
- `GET /api/dossier?mint=`: the fixed coin card, no AI.
- `GET /api/search?q=`: coin search by name, ticker or address.
- Share a coin: `/app?mint=<address>`.

sections.title: Your key
sections.text:
- **Visitors** can paste their own Claude key on `/settings`. It stays in that browser tab (sessionStorage),
  travels with each question in the `x-anthropic-key` header, and is never stored or logged by the server.
- **The site key** is set by the owner behind an admin passcode (stored as a scrypt hash). It is checked with
  one tiny call before it's saved, kept in a `chmod 600` env file, and only ever shown as `…last4`.
- Every log line masks anything shaped like a key. Without a key of their own, visitors share the site key with
  per-IP and daily limits.

sections.title: Honest limits
sections.text:
- **Explains, doesn't predict.** We tested the graph's signals (operator size, two-hop funding, reused socials,
  shared early buyers) against how 23,408 graduated coins did afterwards, using only what was known before each
  graduation. On their own they line up with outcomes (a reused social: −18 points in one-hour survival), but
  they add nothing once a coin's first minutes of trading are known (AUC change within ±0.01). Sniff tells you
  who is behind a coin and what their other coins did. It can't tell you what this one will do.
- **A snapshot.** The graph is built from data recorded up to 2026-10-14 18:45 UTC. Coins launched after that
  aren't in it yet.
- **Coverage.** Many creators have no recorded funder, so "no funder found" can mean we didn't see it, not that
  there wasn't one. Early-buyer data starts on Oct 8.
- Nothing here is financial advice.

written by Claude Code (Anthropic) working under the team's direction. The team chose the problem and
the product, supplied the data from our own pump.fun collector, decided the graph model and its rules

not a prediction"), and reviewed the work, including checking every core query against independent
DuckDB ground truth (`tests/test_queries.py`). The commit history shows the work as it happened during
the event. At runtime, Sniff's answers are written by Claude from the graph's evidence, as described above.

sections.title: Decisions
sections.text:
- **pump.fun only:** a mint must end in `pump` or have its create seen on the pump.fun program. Older collector rows hold other launchpads and existing tokens "reported as new". BONK was one: its record shows a fake 2026-09-20 launch.
- **Hub cut at 200 funded wallets.** Creator share can't tell an exchange from a farm here, because the funder data only covers creators' funders: the largest funder (33,747 wallets) shows 80% creators. Hubs keep their edges plus a `creator_share`, but no query walks through them, and they have no incoming FUNDED edges.
- **Snipers:** each sniper wallet gets an idf weight, `ln(coins sniped / coins this wallet sniped)`. The 603 wallets with more than 100 snipes are `kind = bot` and are ignored by shared-sniper links.
- **Handles:** lowercased; x.com URLs reduced to the handle; X communities kept as their own platform; junk, famous and generic-site stoplists applied. Handles on more than 200 coins count as platforms in `connect`.

sections.title: Memory model and recall
sections.text:
```mermaid
graph LR
  S[Session: random token] -->|ASKED, timestamp| Q[Question: public tool intent]
  Q -->|FOUND, timestamp| E[Evidence: id, tool, summary, observed time]
  E -->|ABOUT| C[Coin: mint]
  E -->|ABOUT| W[Wallet: addr]
  N[Note: by, text, timestamp] -->|ABOUT| C
  N -->|SUPPORTS| E
```

`app/memory.py` records every `/api/ask` investigation and MCP call. It stores the tool intent instead
of the visitor's raw question. A random 32-character token identifies the session; no identity, key,
header or network address is written. The browser receives an HttpOnly `sniff_session` cookie, and JSON,
SSE start/done events and MCP results also return `session_id`. MCP lineage tools accept that token on
follow-ups. The public token acts as a capability to read that session's public graph facts.

Before querying lineage, the tool runner looks for the same tool and exact arguments in that session's
memory. A hit replays the saved result and remaps its local E ids, retaining the original tool and
observed timestamp. Reuse never resets the one-hour freshness window. The agent also reads its session
before planning and can call `memory_recall`. Follow-ups without a mint recover the last investigated
coin. Cross-session recall traverses `Session → Question → Evidence → Coin/Wallet` and groups by tool
and summary; it returns counts and timestamps without session or question identifiers. Counts represent
anonymous sessions, not independent confirmations. No note is promoted to checked lineage evidence.

`memory_note` accepts a self-declared agent label, public text, and optional persistent evidence ids.
Each cited id must already exist and concern the same entity. The graph records `SUPPORTS` links and
labels the note unverified. Another agent can read Sniff's evidence and add its own observation over
the same MCP endpoint. This records coordination and provenance, not authenticated agent identity.

Range indexes cover `Session.sid`, `Question.qid`, `Evidence.eid`, `Evidence.call_key`, `Evidence.at`,
`Coin.mint`, `Wallet.addr` and `Note.nid`. Stored evidence ids are stable UUIDs; `[E#]` ids remain local
to an answer. A failed or privacy-refused memory write is explicitly reported in the response.

sections.text:
The exact local allowlist is `README.md`, `docs/GRAPH.md`, `docs/EVAL.md`, `docs/BLOG.md` and
`docs/PUBLIC-POLICIES.md`. The builder fetches the public homepage's paper/live, safety, pricing and FAQ
sections plus allowlisted public docs. It does not follow arbitrary links, redirects, authenticated
pages, symlinks or recursive docs globs. No handover or infrastructure notes are read.

The public plans, terms and privacy articles currently contain contact email addresses, so their
**entire selected articles are refused**. Public policy summaries cite the original URLs without those
contact details. The audit records only source URL, status and refusal category. It never saves the
matched value. Both the selected raw HTML scope and its extracted text are scanned; secrets hidden in
an attribute or script also refuse that source. Local sources, extraction output and the complete
artifact are scanned again before any load. Matches include API keys, private-key encodings, wallet-key
arrays, seed phrases, emails, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, AWS ids/ARNs and credential assignments.

```mermaid
graph LR
  S[Section] -->|PART_OF| D[Doc: public URL and fetch date]
  S -->|MENTIONS, exact quote| E[Entity]
  E --> P[Product / Feature / Policy]
  E --> F[Decision / Finding / Metric]
  F -->|SUPPORTS / CONTRADICTS / PART_OF / DECIDED_ON| P

provider's tariff; the request and token limits are hard limits. The output records reservations and
failed calls. Each extracted entity name and supporting quote must occur literally in its source;
relationship quotes must also contain both endpoints. Unsupported output is dropped. Unprocessed
sections retain literal source anchors and stay searchable. Each document records its extraction mode.

sections.title: Sniff eval
sections.text:
30 questions in `tests/eval/questions.jsonl`:
- **24 graph questions:** 4 about a coin, 3 each for funding trail, siblings, shared early buyers, shared
  socials and rings, 2 each for links between two things and top operators, and 1 coin search by name.
- **6 to refuse or answer with "no evidence":** will it pump / should I buy, tomorrow's price, "is it safe /
  a scam", "give me coins that will 10x", and 2 addresses that aren't pump.fun launches.

**What each answer is scored on:**
- **tools:** the expected tool was called. For ring questions `coin_dossier` also counts, since it returns the
  creator's ring.
- **citations:** the answer cites at least one real evidence id, with no unknown ids and no id from a tool that
  can't show the claim (`check_citations`). Pure refusals pass when they cite nothing wrong.
- **policy:** the answer ends with the history-not-prediction line and never states buy/sell/safe/scam or a price
  call. Advice words inside a refusal ("I can't say whether it will pump") are allowed. For unknown coins the
  answer must say the coin isn't in the graph.
- **short:** at most 5 sentences before the closing line. This is reported only and is not part of "all three".

sections.title: Who is behind this meme coin? Building Sniff on a graph
sections.text:
*By team QuantBase, for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks, October 2026*

More than ten thousand meme coins launch on pump.fun every day. Almost all of them die within hours. When a new
one shows up on your screen, the question people actually ask isn't "will it go up?", because nobody can
answer that honestly. It's simpler: **who made this, and what happened to the last things they made?**

That question is hard to answer by hand. The wallet that launched the coin is usually brand new. The real
trail runs through whoever paid that wallet to launch it, and through whoever else that payer has paid. That
takes two or three hops of "who sent money to whom", across hundreds of thousands of wallets.

So we built **Sniff**: paste a coin, and an AI agent walks a graph of on-chain history and answers in a few
plain sentences. Every sentence links to the exact part of the graph that proves it.

Try it: https://sniff.quantbase.live/app

sections.title: Why a graph
sections.text:
We already had the raw material. Our QuantBase collector records public pump.fun data: launches, the wallet
behind each one, who funded those wallets, the wallets that bought in the first seconds, and the social links
each coin lists. Before the event it lived in Postgres tables, and every question we asked of it turned into
a tower of self-joins.

The questions are all shaped like paths:

- Who paid the creator? → Who else did that wallet pay? → What did *they* launch? → Did any of it graduate?
- Do these two coins share a funder, an early buyer, or a Twitter account?
- Which wallets form one connected group of launchers?

In FalkorDB each of these is a single Cypher pattern. We loaded 632,339 pump.fun launches, 424,007 wallets and
about 1.5 million relationships (CREATED, FUNDED, SNIPED, LINKS) with the bulk loader in **30 seconds**. The
questions that had been painful became one-liners. Rings of connected launchers come from `algo.WCC`, and
"how are these two connected?" comes from `algo.SPpaths`.

sections.title: Surprise 1: hubs make everything link to everything
sections.text:
The first version of the graph said every coin was connected to every other coin within four hops, which is
true and useless. The reason was exchanges. When a creator withdraws SOL from an exchange, the exchange's hot
wallet shows up as their "funder", and that one wallet funds tens of thousands of creators.

We call these wallets **hubs**: any wallet that funded more than 200 others. There were 89 of them. They get
their own label, keep a note of how many wallets they funded, and **no query is allowed to walk through
them**. A funding trail that reaches a hub stops there and says "this came from an exchange-like wallet, which
tells us nothing about who is behind it."

We tried to be cleverer and tell exchanges apart from big launch farms by what share of their wallets went on
to create coins. It didn't work, because our funding data only covers wallets that created coins. The biggest
hub funded 33,747 wallets and 80% of them were creators, simply because those were the only wallets we had
looked up. So we kept the simple rule, wrote down why, and moved on.

sections.title: Surprise 2: the docs and the database disagreed
sections.text:
FalkorDB 6.0.2 was a pleasure to work with, but a few things in the docs didn't match the running server.
Here's what we hit, so you don't have to:

- **Procedure names:** they differ between pages. On 6.0.2 they are `algo.WCC`, `algo.BFS`, `algo.pageRank`,
  `algo.labelPropagation` and `algo.SPpaths`. `CALL dbms.procedures()` is the source of truth; check it first.
- **Full-text index:** the three-argument `db.idx.fulltext.createNodeIndex('Coin','name','symbol')` from the
  docs is refused. `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX FOR (c:Coin) ON (c.name, c.symbol)` works.
- **`WITH`:** projections need an `AS` alias.
- **Timeouts:** a query timeout can't go above the server's `TIMEOUT_MAX` (15 s by default).
- **Bulk loader:** its default escape character is a backslash, and meme coins are sometimes literally named
  `\`. Pass `-x none` and let your CSV writer double quotes instead.

None of these took long once we knew, and they're all written down in the repo.

sections.title: Surprise 3: one payer, 72 creators, zero graduations
sections.text:
The first time the whole thing ran end to end, we asked about a coin called METHU. Its creator wallet had
launched exactly one coin, which on its own looks like a first-time creator. One hop back told a different story.

The wallet that paid METHU's creator, 0.009 SOL, had paid **71 other brand-new wallets**. Each launched exactly
one coin. **None of the 72 coins graduated.** In the graph it's one funder with 72 spokes, each ending in a
dead coin.

That's the whole idea of Sniff in one picture. The creator alone looks clean; the payer is the story. And you
can only see it if the data is shaped like the question.

sections.title: An agent whose citations are checked
sections.text:
The agent is Claude with nine tools, each a fixed, read-only Cypher query: coin lookup, funding trail,
sibling creators, shared early buyers, shared socials, rings, shortest connection, top operators, and search.
Claude decides which tools to call, up to eight, and writes the answer. It never writes Cypher itself.

Every tool result carries **evidence ids**: E1, E2 and so on. The answer has to end each sentence with the id
that proves it. Then we check:

- A cited id has to be one a tool really returned.
- It has to come from a tool that can show that kind of claim. A sentence about reused socials can't cite
  the funding tool.
- A sentence left with no valid citation is deleted. A shorter answer beats an unsupported one.

In the app, tapping a citation lights up exactly those wallets and coins on the map. If there's no AI key, or
the AI call fails, the same tools produce a fixed summary instead, so the facts never depend on the model.

We scored it on 30 questions, including six it should refuse ("will this pump?", "is it safe?", made-up
addresses). On the live site all 10 questions we spent real calls on picked the right tools, cited valid
evidence and stayed within the no-advice rule. What failed was length: half the answers ran past five
sentences, so answers are now capped at five.

sections.title: The honest part: it explains, it doesn't predict
sections.text:
We also run trading research on the same data, so we asked the uncomfortable question: do these graph
signals help predict which coins do well after graduating?

We built the features strictly as they would have been known at the moment each coin graduated: how many
other creators the funder paid, two-hop funding, reused socials, shared early buyers. Then we tested them on
23,408 graduated coins, training on the older ones and testing on the newest third.

On their own, the signals mean something. Coins whose social account had been used on another creator's coin
were 18 points less likely to still be alive an hour later. But once you add what anyone can already see in a
coin's first couple of minutes of trading, the graph adds **nothing measurable**: the change in predictive
accuracy was within ±0.01. Whatever the graph knows has already shown up in the price.

So Sniff doesn't say "safe" or "scam", and it never says buy or sell. It tells you who is behind a coin and
what their other coins did, with receipts, and ends every answer with the same line: *history, not a
prediction.* We think that's the honest version of this product, and the useful one.

sections.text:
- Evidence. How a launch filled, what the creator did before, whether the
coin is a copy, and how coins of the same kind did one hour, six hours and
a day after graduating. Every rate carries its sample size.

- Exit discipline. Rules you choose before you buy: sell half at 2x, trail
the rest, cut at half, leave after six hours, get out if the pool drains.
The coach checks every minute and tells you when one fires.

sections.title: What it is not#
sections.text:
- Not buy signals. No picks, no price targets, no "gems". The feed lists
what graduated and the facts about it. It never says what to buy.

- Not advice. Nothing on QuantBase is investment, financial or trading
advice. Past rates may not repeat.

- Not a trading terminal. QuantBase places no trades for you, holds none of
your coins and never asks for your keys. Selling stays your decision.

- Not paid per trade. You pay a flat monthly price. QuantBase earns
nothing when you trade, so telling you not to buy costs it nothing.

sections.title: Quickstart
sections.text:
Sign in, read the feed, open a coin, and put the exit coach on a coin you bought.

This takes about five minutes. Steps 1, 3 and 6 are free. Steps 2, 4 and 5
need the Meme plan ($19 a month).

sections.title: 1. Sign in#
sections.text:
Open app.quantbase.live.

- With a Solana wallet. Choose Continue with your wallet (any wallet
that supports the Wallet Standard, such as Phantom, Solflare or Backpack).
Your wallet asks you to sign a short text message. It is text, not a
transaction: it costs nothing and moves no funds. The same button creates
your account the first time.

- With an email account. Use the sign-in form under "Signed up with
Google or email before? Continue here."

Details: Sign-in.

sections.title: 2. Read the feed#
sections.text:
The console opens on Home. The Just graduated list shows pump.fun
coins that graduated in the last 24 hours and were worth $150K or more, in a
funded pool, two minutes after graduating. Each coin carries a chip:
Avoid, a warning count such as 1 warning, or Looks clean. Home
hides coins the scorecard blocks and says why, under a "Why ... were hidden"
link; Coins shows them all.

Without the Meme plan, the console shows "Part of the Meme plan" here. The
homepage at quantbase.live shows the same
kind of list, delayed 10 minutes, free.

sections.title: 3. Open a coin#
sections.text:
Tap a coin, or paste any coin address into Paste a coin address… at the
top of the console. The coin page shows:

- Lens evidence: the verdict and flags, the creator and their funding
cluster, and the base rates. Free.

- A price chart (1m, 5m, 15m) and How coins like it did: coins of the same
kind, size and pool, one hour, six hours and a day later. Meme plan.

What each part means: Coin evidence.

sections.title: 4. Tell the coach what you bought#
sections.text:
QuantBase never buys for you. Buy where you normally do, then come back and
choose I bought this on the coin page (or Add a coin I bought on
Home).

Field
What to enter

The mint, usually ending in pump

Price you paid, in USD

Choose Start watching it. The coach prices the coin every minute against
your exit rules. On the coin page your levels are drawn on the chart: entry,
the half-sell level, the trailing stop and the cut.

Before your first coin, check My exit rules (on Me, or
Settings → Exit rules). The defaults are: sell half at 2x, protect the
rest once it is up 30% by selling if it falls 30% from its best, always sell
at −50%, close after 6 hours, and leave if the pool drains under $1,000. A
change applies to coins you add from then on.

sections.title: Exit coach
sections.text:
Set your exit before you buy. The coach watches every coin you tell it about, every minute, and tells you which rule fired. It never sells for you.

Most coins that double give the gain back within hours. The coach exists so
that the decision to leave is made in advance, as a rule, instead of in the
moment. It is part of the Meme plan.

sections.title: What it never does#
sections.text:
- It never buys or sells. QuantBase has no access to your wallet, exchange
account or keys, and the coach places no orders anywhere.

- It never tells you what to buy. It only watches coins you already hold.

- It never assumes you sold. A sale counts only when you record it.

A rule firing is a statement about the price. Whether you sell is your
decision.

sections.title: How a rule fires#
sections.text:
- Every minute, the coach reads each coin's price and pool liquidity from
DexScreener, at its deepest Solana pool, and updates the best price seen.

- It checks the rules in this order: pool drained, sell half, trailing stop,
cut, time stop. The first one that applies fires.

- It writes an alert with the rule and the numbers, for example "fell 31%
from its peak (2.40x → 1.66x). Sell the rest now."

- Sell half moves the coin on: the trailing stop and the other rules keep
watching the rest. Any other rule closes the coin in the coach.

Between checks the console may already show a rule as due: the price is
past it and the coach will fire it on its next check.

On the coin, each rule shows its state: waiting (not in play yet, such as
a trailing stop that has not armed), armed, due, fired or
done (you recorded the sale). The one nearest to firing is shown first.

If DexScreener has no price for a coin in a given minute, that coin is
skipped for the minute.

sections.title: Recording what you did#
sections.text:
On the coin, I sold half and I sold it all record a sale at the
current price. They sell nothing. Recording half also stops the 2x alert;
recording the rest closes the coin. Over MCP you can give the exact price you
sold at.

Trade history shows closed coins with your entry, the peak, your exits,
Peak kept (how much of the gain at the peak you actually kept) and what
closed it: a rule, or you. Where you did not record a sale, the rest is
valued at the last price when the coin closed and marked as assumed.

sections.title: Alerts#
sections.text:
Every alert lands in Alerts in the console, newest first, with a bell
count in the header. Tabs: All, Exits, Rugs, Graduates,
Unread. Mark all read clears the count.

Kind
When

Exit
Sell half, trailing stop, cut or time stop fired

Rug
The pool drained under your limit

Watchlist
You added a coin: the levels it will be watched at

Daily summary
Once a day at 03:30 UTC, if you had activity: alerts, exits, how much of each peak you kept, what is still open

Graduate, Note, Notice
Other notices on your account

sections.title: Telegram#
sections.text:
Under Me → Alerts (or Settings), choose Get a link code. You get
a one-time code, valid for one hour, to send to the QuantBase bot as
/start <code>. When the account is linked, each alert kind you have chosen
is sent to that chat; Unlink stops it.

The console currently says the customer bot is not live yet. Keep the code;
it links your account when the bot opens. Until then, alerts reach you in the
console inbox only. Alerts that could not be delivered within two hours are
not sent late. Email alerts are not available.

sections.title: Limits of the coach#
sections.text:
- It checks once a minute. A coin can move a long way inside a minute, and a
pool can drain between two checks.

- DexScreener's price is not your fill. Slippage and fees are not included in
any multiple the coach shows.

- The rules limit losses and keep part of a win. They do not make a bad coin
good, and they lose money on coins that never take off.

Evidence, not advice. The coach reports that a rule fired. It does not
recommend a trade.
